NEW DELHI: Jai Moondra's cricket journey has come full circle.Just days after making a dream T20I debut against India, the Rajasthan - born fast bowler has now added another milestone to his rapidly rising career by making his ODI debut for Ireland in the five - match series against Afghanistan.The 29-year-old has already announced himself on the international stage. In his maiden T20I series against the country he once dreamed of representing, Moondra made an immediate impact.He dismissed Sanju Samson with the very first ball of his international career in the opening T20I before removing Shivam Dube to claim his second wicket.In the second T20I, he dismissed Samson for a duck once again, making the India opener his bunny. He also removed Abhishek Sharma for a duck and Shreyas Iyer for 10 to finish with figures of 3/32 and help Ireland register a famous 2 - 0 series win.His impressive performances against India quickly sparked curiosity. Questions flooded social media: Who is Jai Moondra? Who is this India - born cricketer?The answer begins thousands of kilometres away from Dublin, in Tonk, Rajasthan.When Moondra left India to pursue higher studies in Ireland, he did not just leave his family behind.He also left behind his first love - cricket.Moondra moved to Ireland to pursue a Master's degree in Electronics and Communication at Technological University Dublin. But whenever he saw children playing cricket in parks or small grounds across Dublin, he would stop for a moment. He would watch them appeal loudly, celebrate wickets, run between the wickets, bowl with long run - ups and dive to save runs. Then he would quietly walk away with a backpack full of books on his shoulders - shoulders that once carried a cricket kit bag.Moondra may have left cricket in India, but cricket never left him.Moondra continued chasing coding deadlines at work while also keeping his cricket dream alive at Leinster Cricket Club (LCC) in Dublin.Eventually, the dream he had left behind in India was fulfilled in Ireland when he received his debut cap for Ireland against the team he had once dreamed of representing - India.Few know that there is a Pakistani connection behind Moondra's rise.Moondra learnt the art of swing and pace from Bilal Azhar, a left - arm fast bowler from Islamabad, Pakistan, who moved to Ireland in 2008.Moondra met Bilal after he resumed playing cricket at Leinster Cricket Club in Dublin.Bilal, who idolised Wasim Akram and was himself a left - arm pacer, spotted something special in Moondra during a pre - season net session.Office, cricket, sleep and repeat - that became Moondra's routine. Throughout that journey, Bilal remained one of the biggest influences in the young pacer's career.“He just came in and bowled. I was batting that day, and I felt there were some quick balls there. We knew immediately - there is something in this boy,” Bilal told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview from Dublin.“He was definitely quick, but he was bowling too many no - balls. We worked on simple drills. It was just about controlling that pace. He is a quick learner. He listens. He works hard. Even in the off - season, he used to train with parachute runs just to bowl faster,” Bilal added.For Bilal, Jai's debut against India was hardly a surprise.“It didn’t even feel like a debut. We always knew since 2024–25 that he is special. There were no nerves. When a bowler is hitting 142 - plus clicks and dismissing top - quality batters, you don’t talk about nerves. You talk about quality. Jai is calm - he performs quietly and lets his bowling do the talking. He performs silently. He is there or thereabouts with that kind of raw pace you associate with bowlers like Wasim Akram or Waqar Younis," he said."He told me about the selection before it was officially announced. We just told him - go and enjoy it. He is very calm by nature. He treats every match like just another game,” he said.While Bilal helped polish Moondra's skills in Ireland, the foundation of his bowling had already been laid in India under former Ranji cricketer Mohan Singh at SS Cricket Club in Jaipur.Moondra trained under Mohan before leaving for Ireland, and the coach believes the fast bowler's success is the result of years of hard work and discipline.“He came to us for bowling tips in 2017. His speed was dropping. We corrected his foot position and body alignment. He worked very hard - very disciplined,” said Mohan Singh.Mohan recalled that even when Moondra decided to move abroad for higher studies and a job, he encouraged him not to give up cricket.“That dedication was always there - studying, coming on time, following discipline. Even during COVID, he kept working. He told me he had to go for studies and a job. I told him - if you get a chance in Ireland, don’t leave cricket,” Mohan said.Moondra also stayed connected with his coach after earning his Ireland call - up.“He is emotional, honest, and very respectful. And he even called me after selection. That matters more than anything,” Mohan added.If Moondra's cricketing foundation was laid in India, it was shaped in Dublin.At Leinster Cricket Club (LCC), Moondra received everything he needed to continue his cricket journey - from bats and kit to training facilities, nets and flexible schedules. A major reason behind that support was first - team manager Michael Colleran.While Bilal worked on Moondra's bowling, Colleran ensured the 29 - year - old had the right environment to grow as a cricketer.Colleran recalled how the club first got to know Moondra.“Bilal insisted we give him the ball. He believed in him from day one. We worked on his workload and fitness. He is a student of the game and improves every season,” Colleran said."When he first came, he looked like a rookie but he was not. He knew his game; all we did was polish and work on certain things. With time, he evolved as a player. We at LCC are so proud of him. The way he managed his job and practice was amazing. A punctual and hard - working guy," he said.When Moondra finally earned his Ireland debut, the advice from the club was simple.“We told him - just enjoy it. He is very humble and very level - headed,” Colleran said.Moondra's debut changed everything for LCCFor Leinster Cricket Club, Moondra's international debut has become much more than a personal achievement. His success has generated fresh excitement around the club, with more youngsters showing interest in taking up cricket.Suyash Vaidya, chairman of the LCC senior men's team, said Moondra's rise has inspired the next generation of cricketers.“With his talent and fast - bowling ability, he has become one of the stars of our club. He has also become an inspiration for our youth players and for everyone across LCC who comes to watch him perform,” Vaidya said.“His selection in the international team has created huge excitement among our students, juniors, and players, and even across our social media followers. We’ve seen a big rise in interest, and day by day we are receiving more inquiries and requests to join the club,” he said.Having already made memorable start to his T20I carrer , Moondra now enters the next phase of his international journey with growing expectations.From the technical corrections under Mohan Singh in Jaipur to the polishing of his skills under Bilal Azhar in Dublin, and the backing of Leinster Cricket Club, every step helped shape the fast bowler who is now living the dream he once thought he had left behind in India.
Article Summary: Jai Moondra made his ODI debut for Ireland in the five - match series against Afghanistan. The Rajasthan - born fast bowler has already announced himself on the international stage. He dismissed Sanju Samson with the very first ball of his international career in the opening T20I before removing Shivam Dube.

Article Title: 'Unnecessary pressure': Ex-cricketer questions Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's elevation to vice-captaincy
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Gujarat captain Priyank Panchal has become the latest voice to question the decision to appoint 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as East Zone vice-captain for the upcoming Duleep Trophy, saying the teenager should first be allowed to settle into the demands of red-ball cricket.Sooryavanshi, who will serve as deputy to Ishan Kishan , was handed the leadership role despite having played only eight first-class matches for Bihar. His appointment came ahead of far more experienced players, including Abhimanyu Easwaran, who has featured in 113 first-class games.The decision followed Sooryavanshi's impressive outing in Zimbabwe, where he was named Player of the Series after scoring 151 runs in three T20Is, including a match-winning 81 in the third and final game.However, Panchal believes the selectors could have waited before entrusting the youngster with additional responsibility."I think the zonal selectors could have avoided making Vaibhav Sooryavanshi the East Zone vice captain. It could put unnecessary pressure on the young kid. Let him understand the dynamics of red ball cricket first, properly, before entrusting such duties upon him. Thoughts? #DuleepTrophy," Panchal wrote on X (formerly Twitter).The appointment has sparked debate among fans and former cricketers, with many arguing that the teenager should be given time to develop before taking on a leadership role in one of India's premier domestic red-ball tournaments.Despite the criticism, East Zone selectors have defended the decision, insisting it is part of a long-term plan for Sooryavanshi's development."We are not thinking about the present alone," Manish Vardhan, former cricketer and Jharkhand's representative on the East Zone selection committee, told Cricinfo."A vice-captain gets to observe the captain closely and understand how a team is run. We wanted Vaibhav to be more involved with the group because we think it will help him as he develops. He's an extremely talented cricketer and is maturing steadily. Giving him this responsibility is another part of that process," he added.The 63rd edition of the Duleep Trophy begins on August 23 at the BCCI 's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru. East Zone will face North-East Zone in the opening round, while West Zone take on North Zone. The winners will meet South Zone and Central Zone respectively in the semi-finals on August 30, with the final scheduled for September 5.
Article Summary: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi named East Zone vice-captain for upcoming Duleep Trophy. Former Gujarat captain Priyank Panchal questions decision to appoint teenager. Teenager has played only eight first-class matches for Bihar. East Zone selectors have defended the decision, insisting it is part of a long-term plan.

Article Title: 'He was my sponsor': How Virat Kohli helped CWG gold medallist Sakshi Chaudhary
Article Text:
Virat Kohli and Sakshi Chaudhary (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Days after scripting history with a gold medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games, Indian boxer Sakshi Chaudhary has revealed the role former India captain Virat Kohli played in her journey to the top.The Haryana boxer, who clinched gold in the women's 51kg (Flyweight) event in Glasgow, said Kohli supported her through the Virat Kohli Foundation during a crucial phase of her career and credited him for helping her stay focused.Speaking to IANS, Sakshi thanked Kohli for backing her, saying the cricket icon's support extended beyond sponsorship."I started boxing after watching Vijender Singh , but in my journey, Virat Kohli has also supported me a lot. He has been my sponsor. So I would like to thank him too," Chaudhary said.She added that Kohli also motivated her with simple advice, encouraging her to stay calm, avoid taking pressure and focus only on performing inside the ring.Sakshi's triumph in Glasgow capped a remarkable comeback. Having missed the 2022 Commonwealth Games and the 2023 Asian Games due to injury, she made the calculated decision to drop from the 54kg category to 51kg, a gamble that ultimately earned her the biggest medal of her career.The Indian Army boxer defeated England's Ruby White by a unanimous 5-0 decision in the final to claim the gold medal.Sakshi was one of the standout performers in India's historic boxing campaign, which produced 10 medals, including a record seven golds. Alongside her, world champion Jaismine Lamboria, Preeti Pawar (54kg), Priya Ghanghas (60kg), Arundhati Choudhary (70kg), Sachin Siwach (60kg) and Ankush Panghal (80kg) finished on top of the podium, while Lovlina Borgohain, Jadumani Singh and Narender Berwal added silver medals.No nation has won more boxing gold medals than India's tally of seven at a single edition of the Commonwealth Games.
Article Summary: Sakshi Chaudhary thanks Virat Kohli for backing her in her boxing career. The Haryana boxer won gold in the women's 51kg (Flyweight) event in Glasgow. Sakshi was one of the standout performers in India's historic boxing campaign, which produced 10 medals, including seven golds.

Article Title: From hospital bed to CWG gold: How Jaismine Lamboria fought the odds in Glasgow
Article Text:
India's Jaismine Lamboria celebrates after winning the women's 57kg boxing final. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Just weeks before stepping into the ring at the Commonwealth Games, Jaismine Lamboria wasn’t thinking about medals. She was searching for answers. The recurring fever had refused to go away.Multiple medical tests showed nothing unusual and the Indian boxer tried to push through, managing the symptoms with paracetamol. When the illness persisted, she was admitted to a hospital in Mohali. Doctors finally diagnosed a bacterial infection, putting her on an intensive 14-day course of medication. For an athlete preparing for one of the biggest competitions of the year, it could easily have been the end of the campaign.Instead, it became the beginning of one of the most remarkable comebacks of her career. “I was avoiding further medical tests because the initial reports were coming back normal. We didn’t know what exactly had to be treated. Finally, after I was admitted, they detected a bacterial infection and I was on medication for 14 days,” the 57kg boxer said.When she was discharged, the clock was already ticking. Barely three weeks remained before the Games.“I started training only on July 1. Initially it was just warm-up, walking and stretching. I had very little time, so we had to be patient.”The physical recovery was only one part of the challenge. During those uncertain weeks, sports psychologist Priya Vrinda became a constant source of support, ensuring the illness didn’t break her confidence.“When I was sick, I was already connected with Priya Vrinda ma’am. She kept me mentally strong and never allowed me to go down,” Jaismine said. That resilience was evident when she returned to competition. Jaismine boxed with maturity, tactical discipline and composure to upgrade the Commonwealth bronze she had won four years ago into gold in the 57kg.One of Jaismine’s biggest assets inside the ring has been her reach in her category. While every opponent may not be shorter — Jaismine stands five feet seven inches in her socks — she believes her physical advantage has become an important weapon thanks to careful coaching. “My coaches taught me how to use my reach properly. It definitely gives me an advantage in many bouts.”
Article Summary: Jaismine Lamboria won gold in the women's 57kg boxing at the Commonwealth Games. The Indian boxer had been suffering from a recurring fever. Doctors diagnosed a bacterial infection and put her on a 14-day course of medication. Jaismine credits her coach Priya Vrinda with helping her recover.

Article Title: Days after historic CWG gold, Dilip Gavit leaves without meeting Raj Thackeray after two-hour wait
Article Text:
India's Dilip Mahadu Gavit (PTI Photo)

Invited, but left waiting

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A champion who made history in Glasgow

A journey built on resilience

Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a very different reason. The 23-year-old sprinter, who became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event, waited for nearly two hours to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray in Nashik on Thursday before leaving without the meeting taking place.According to Gavit's coach quoted by PTI, Vaijanath Kale, the para-athlete had been invited to meet Thackeray during the MNS chief's visit to Nashik. However, despite arriving at the scheduled venue, Gavit and his coach were made to wait for nearly two hours. A video from the venue showed MNS workers requesting the duo to wait longer while trying to explain that Thackeray was occupied."We were waiting for quite some time... Sir is busy. We will meet him later," Kale is heard saying in the video before they eventually left.The incident came just days after Gavit delivered one of India's biggest moments at the Commonwealth Games. Clocking a Games-record 10.71 seconds, the Nashik sprinter won the men's 100m T47 gold medal, leading a historic Indian one-two finish alongside Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath, who claimed silver. The victory marked India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics 100m T47.Gavit's success carries a deeper significance given his remarkable journey. Born into an economically disadvantaged tribal family in Maharashtra, he lost his right arm in a childhood accident. His life changed when coach Vaijanath Kale took him under his wing at the age of 12, supporting his education and athletic development. After winning gold in Glasgow, Gavit emotionally dedicated the medal to Kale, crediting his coach for transforming his life.
Article Summary: Dilip Gavit was invited to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray. The 23-year-old sprinter waited for nearly two hours for the meeting to take place. The incident came just days after he became India's first Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event.

Article Title: 'I worked tirelessly while staying in Pakistan': Arshad Nadeem blames Glasgow cold for CWG poor show
Article Text:
Arshad Nadeem (AFP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lausanne Diamond League next

Pakistan’s Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem has blamed the cold Glasgow weather for his disappointing performance at the Commonwealth Games. The defending champion finished ninth after failing to make the final three rounds, saying the low temperature made his body stiff and affected his usually smooth run-up.Nadeem managed 77.41 metres with his second throw after opening with a foul. His third attempt was 75.39m, leaving him outside the top eight.“The weather was extremely cold and I personally felt that it affected my body. As you have seen in many of my previous competitions, my run-up is usually very smooth, but this time it wasn’t… because my body had become stiff due to the cold conditions. My fitness was good and my health was fine, but ultimately whatever Allah wills is what happens,” he told reporters on Wednesday.Despite the result, Nadeem said he remains determined to make a strong comeback and urged fans to continue supporting him.“Please don’t lose heart and don’t stop supporting me either. Whatever I have achieved has only been possible because Allah blessed me with the opportunity to do it. The respect and recognition Pakistan has received around the world have come through years of hard work. I worked tirelessly while staying in Pakistan,” he added.“God willing, I will prepare with full dedication for the upcoming competitions and once again raise Pakistan’s flag on the international stage.”Nadeem also responded to criticism on social media, saying he understood the disappointment among Pakistani fans.“I have heard many things on social media, but I want everyone to remember that I am Pakistan’s son, and I always will be,” he maintained.Nadeem’s next challenge will be the Lausanne Diamond League in Switzerland on August 21. He will face a strong field that includes India’s Neeraj Chopra , Commonwealth champion Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage, Keshorn Walcott, Anderson Peters and Thomas Rohler.Nadeem will hope to regain his form before the Asian Games later this year.
Article Summary: Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem has blamed the cold Glasgow weather for his disappointing performance at the Commonwealth Games. The defending champion finished ninth after failing to make the final three rounds. He said the low temperature made his body stiff and affected his usually smooth run-up.

Article Title: Glasgow to Ahmedabad: Gujarat receives Commonwealth Games flag as 2030 countdown begins
Article Text:
Neeraj Chopra, left, hands over the Commonwealth Games Federation flag to Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president P T Usha during the closing ceremony of the 23rd Commonwealth Games (CWG), at OVO Hydro, in Glasgow, Scotland. (PTI)

The Commonwealth Games flag was formally presented to Gujarat chief minister Bhupendra Patel on Wednesday, marking the beginning of preparations for the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad.After returning from Glasgow, deputy chief minister Harsh Sanghavi handed over the flag to Patel during the state cabinet meeting in Gandhinagar.Sanghavi had attended the closing ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Sunday along with Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president PT Usha. During the ceremony, the Commonwealth Games flag was officially handed over to India as Ahmedabad prepares to host the next edition in 2030.According to an official release, "deputy chief minister Harsh Sanghavi formally presented the Commonwealth Games Flag, with full honour and dignity, to chief minister Bhupendra Patel during the state cabinet meeting in Gandhinagar."Para-athletes Rakesh Bhatt and Rohit Majgul, who represented Gujarat at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, were present during the ceremony. Along with advancing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 'Fit India' vision, it will serve as an inspiration for athletes and symbolise the commencement of preparations for the upcoming event."Speaking to reporters after arriving at Ahmedabad Airport earlier in the day, Sanghavi said the city aims to set a new standard for hosting the Commonwealth Games."These Games will be organised with grandeur and with the best possible arrangements for the athletes. They will be conducted in such a way that every athlete can deliver his best performance," the deputy CM said.Sanghavi, who also holds the sports portfolio, said the Gujarat government remains committed to taking forward Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Fit India movement and anti-drug campaign."We will advance the anti-drug campaign and the Fit India Movement so that the youth of the country receive maximum opportunities in the sports sector. The Gujarat Government is working towards this goal. Under the guidance of the Government of India, we will continue to move this work forward," he said.
Article Summary: The Commonwealth Games flag was formally presented to Gujarat chief minister Bhupendra Patel on Wednesday. Deputy chief minister Harsh Sanghavi handed over the flag to Patel during the state cabinet meeting in Gandhinagar. Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president PT Usha attended the ceremony.

Article Title: Reality check after Commonwealth Games 2026: India’s boxing renaissance to face ultimate Asian exam
Article Text:
New Delhi, Aug 04 (ANI): Union Minister Kiren Rijiju in a group photograph with Indian boxing contingent (@KirenRijiju X/ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s record-breaking boxing campaign at the Commonwealth Games has generated plenty of optimism, but the celebrations will quickly give way to a far sterner test when attention shifts to the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from Sept 19 to Oct 4. After returning from Glasgow with a historic haul of seven gold and three silver medals, India’s boxers now head into what many within the sport regard as the closest thing to the Olympics.The CWG triumph underlined the country’s growing depth, particularly in women’s boxing. Sakshi Chaudhary (51kg), Preeti Pawar (54kg), Jaismine Lamboria (57kg), Priya Ghanghas (60kg) and Arundhati Choudhary (70kg) struck gold, while Sachin Siwach (60kg) and Ankush Panghal (80kg) topped the podium in the men’s competition. Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain, Jadumani Singh and Narender Berwal added silver medals.The challenge in Aichi-Nagoya, however, will be on an entirely different scale. Unlike the Commonwealth Games, the Asian Games will feature continental powerhouses such as Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, China, Chinese Taipei, Japan and North Korea — nations that have consistently dominated the World Championships and the Olympics.Uzbek stars Mirazizbek Mirzakhalilov and Bobo-Usmon Baturov, along with Kazakhstan’s Kairat Yeraliyev and Ablaikhan Zhussupov, are expected to headline a field packed with world-class talent.India will also be without two of its Commonwealth champions. Jaismine (57kg) and Arundhati (70kg) will miss out because their weight categories do not feature in the Asian Games programme, depriving the country of two genuine medal prospects.“The Asian Games for us is like the Olympics,” Boxing Federation of India president Ajay Singh said. “The best teams in the world today are Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and India, and all three are in Asia. Add a strong Chinese contingent and you understand why it is much tougher. You can’t replicate this (CWG) performance at the Asian Games. But if you win a sizeable number of medals at the Asian Games, you can be hopeful of winning medals at the Olympics too.Women’s head coach Santiago Nieva shared a similar assessment while insisting the team remains on the right path.“We can’t guarantee that we will win gold all the time, but we are on the right track. We know how strong the field will be at the Asian Games. The boxers are aware that they can’t sit on their success,” he said.India had returned with one silver and three bronze medals from the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. The Glasgow CWG showcased the strides the boxing contingent has made. But it’ll be Aichi-Nagoya that is going to reveal whether the progress is enough to challenge Asia’s finest and signal genuine medal potential for the 2028 Olympics.
Article Summary: India's record-breaking boxing campaign at the Commonwealth Games has generated plenty of optimism. But the celebrations will quickly give way to a far sterner test when attention shifts to the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from Sept 19 to Oct 4. India’s boxers now head into what many within the sport regard as the closest thing to the Olympics.

Article Title: Pakistan boxer Qudratullah ‘goes missing’ in Glasgow after Commonwealth Games campaign
Article Text:
Pakistan boxer Qudratullah

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistani boxer Qudratullah has reportedly gone missing in Glasgow, just hours before the country’s Commonwealth Games contingent was scheduled to leave for home.According to a report by Pakistani outlet Geo News, sources in the Pakistan Boxing Federation said Qudratullah was last seen in his hotel room at around 2am. Officials later checked his room and found that he was no longer there.The Pakistan team was due to gather in the hotel lobby at 9am before leaving for Pakistan. However, Qudratullah could not be found when officials checked his room, sources said.His passport and return ticket are reportedly still with the team manager. The incident is not the first such case involving a Pakistani boxer abroad, with another promising boxer, Zohaib, reportedly going missing during an international tour of Italy last year.Pakistan’s 21-member contingent finished the 2026 Commonwealth Games with only one medal. Boxer Fatima Zahra won bronze in the women’s 60kg category, giving Pakistan its only podium finish at the Games.The result was Pakistan’s lowest medal tally since the 1998 Commonwealth Games, when the country won one silver. Pakistan had also returned without a medal from the 1990 edition, making Glasgow its poorest CWG campaign in 36 years.Fatima made history by becoming the first Pakistani female boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal and was later chosen to carry the national flag at the closing ceremony.Pakistan’s biggest medal hope, Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem, also failed to finish on the podium after serving as the country’s flagbearer at the opening ceremony.
Article Summary: Qudratullah was last seen in his hotel room at around 2am. Pakistan team was due to gather in the hotel lobby at 9am before leaving for Pakistan. Pakistan’s 21-member contingent finished the 2026 Commonwealth Games with only one medal.

Article Title: ‘Like preparing for IIT and UPSC together’: Father Murali shares Sreeshankar’s comeback story
Article Text:
Murali Sreeshankar

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOCHI: S Murali gave an unusual analogy to describe the struggles his son, long jumper Sreeshankar Murali, undertook to regain full fitness after a career-threatening knee injury he sustained two years ago.“Sreeshankar’s comeback was as difficult as preparing for the IIT and Civil Services simultaneously,” he told TOI.Murali is currently near Prague, where he is closely monitoring his son’s training ahead of a busy stretch that begins with the World Athletics Continental Tour (silver level) meet in Bhubaneswar on Aug 22, followed by next month’s Asian Games in Japan.“Sreeshankar’s training now revolves around strength and conditioning, along with the prehab and rehab programme designed by coach Wayne Lombard. There is very little time to work on technique. The priority is to protect the knee on his take-off leg,” Murali said.His IIT-UPSC analogy aptly captures the magnitude of the challenge Sreeshankar faced after suffering the devastating injury just months before the 2024 Paris Olympics.Two years later, the journey came full circle when the 27-year-old clinched the silver medal at last week’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.“Of all the medals Sreeshankar has won, this one gives me the greatest satisfaction because of the circumstances under which he achieved it. It reflects his mental toughness and hunger,” Murali said.The conditions in Glasgow were anything but favourable.“It was around 12 degrees Celsius with drizzle and strong winds, making the runway tricky,” Murali said. Despite the difficult conditions, Sreeshankar produced a best jump of 8.09m to finish second.The performance inevitably brought back painful memories of 2024, when the family received a grim diagnosis after Sreeshankar tore the patellar tendon in his take-off leg.“The doctors in Mumbai had not seen an injury like this. I thought he would never be able to walk again,” Murali recalled.“They told us it wasn’t a common sports injury but the kind usually seen after a serious car accident. His knee was completely ruptured.”Determined to find the best treatment, Murali travelled nearly 1,900 miles with his son to Doha’s Aspetar Hospital. “The surgeons reconstructed his knee using four screws.”The Palakkad athlete spent more than eight months away from competition before beginning the long rehabilitation process.The painstaking recovery paid rich dividends. Since returning to elite competition, Sreeshankar has consistently cleared the eight-metre mark, including a season’s best of 8.38m at the Inter-State Championships in Bhubaneswar in June.“There is no time to bask in the Commonwealth Games glory,” Murali said, pointing to the demanding schedule ahead.Sreeshankar will now turn his attention to the Asian Games in Japan, where he hopes to upgrade the silver medal he won at the previous edition in Hangzhou.“With everything Sreeshankar has gone through, he has every reason to believe he can stand on top of the podium at the Asian Games,” Murali concluded.
Article Summary: Sreeshankar Murali suffered a career-threatening knee injury two years ago. The Palakkad athlete spent more than eight months away from competition before beginning the long rehabilitation process. The 27-year-old clinched the silver medal at last week's Commonwealth Games.

Article Title: 'You are still a role model': CWG medallist Tejaswin Shankar hails Vinesh Phogat, recalls 2018 memories
Article Text:
Tejaswin Shankar and Vinesh Phogat

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Vinesh Phogat to challenge Brij Bhushan acquittal

Commonwealth Games 2026 bronze medallist Tejaswin Shankar has expressed his gratitude to star wrestler Vinesh Phogat for her words of encouragement after a knee injury forced him to withdraw from the high jump event at the recent Commonwealth Games.Shankar, a two-time Commonwealth Games medallist, was forced out of the high jump after his long-standing knee problem flared up during his opening attempt. The setback left the athlete devastated, with Shankar breaking down in tears after being unable to continue.Despite the disappointment, he bounced back strongly in the gruelling two-day decathlon, finishing with 7,976 points and securing his second Commonwealth Games medal. His national record in the decathlon stands at 8,057 points.Shankar has been dealing with chronic patellar tendinitis, commonly known as jumper’s knee.Following his withdrawal, Vinesh had reached out to him with a motivational message, urging him to remain focused and prepared for whatever came next.“Teju, you still can do it. Stay focused on what is ahead," Vinesh wrote on X. "My coach always said, as professional athletes, we must always be prepared for the best and at the same time, be ready for the worst.In life, everything happened for a reason, I guess. Rooting for you as always."Remembering Vinesh’s support, Shankar thanked her publicly and recalled how she had helped him feel comfortable during his first Commonwealth Games in 2018.Remembering her support, Shankar replied, “Thank you, Vinesh ji for your motivating words. I remember my first CWG in 2018 as a teenager when you made me feel comfortable and told me that I belonged there. 8 years later, you are still a role model."Meanwhile, Vinesh said the women wrestlers who accused former Wrestling Federation of India chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh of sexual harassment will appeal a Delhi court’s decision to acquit him.A Delhi court on Monday acquitted Brij Bhushan and co-accused Vinod Tomar in the sexual harassment case filed by the women wrestlers. India finished the 2026 Commonwealth Games with 39 medals to its name - 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze. It placed India in fourth place behind Australia, England and Canada. Boxing and athletics produced the most medals (10) with weightlifting (8) and para-athletics (6) next in the order.In the truncated quadrennial event, held without shooting, wrestling, badminton, table tennis and field hockey, all of which have contributed significantly to India's coffers in the past, the country finished with 22 medals fewer than the 2022 edition in Birmingham (61 medals).Gulveer Singh emerged as the only multiple medallist for India at the Games. His silver in 10,000m and bronze in 5,000m made him the first Indian track and field athlete to win two individual medals at a single CWG edition.The Aligarh-born Naib Subedar made his international breakthrough with a bronze medal in the 5000m at the 2023 Asian Athletics Championships and followed it up with another third-place finish at the rescheduled 2022 Asian Games.The 28-year-old national record holder in 5000m, 10,000m, one mile and half-marathon trains regularly at the high-performance centre in Colorado Springs, USA, where steps towards his multiple feats and medals are forged.A Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) athlete, he's been assisted with Rs 30.40 lakh during this CWG cycle and Rs 25.32 lakh under the Annual Calendar for Training and Competition (ACTC).Behind every medal is days and weeks of training and preparation backed by government and funding by private players.Before the Glasgow Games got underway, the track and field athletes and para-athletes underwent training at the Spala Olympic Training Centre in Poland; boxers spent time in Belfast; the lifters travelled to Birmingham while the Artistic Gymnastics team set camp in South Essex.All such tours were sponsored by the government through its ACTC fund and TOPS.TOPS, a division formed in September 2014, operates as the Sports Ministry's flagship programme to support India's athletes win medals at the Olympics. It is presently headed by Col. Nachhatar Singh Johal, who represented the country in sailing at the 2008 Beijing Olympics.Earlier this year, TOPS' ambit increased to 27 sports with six getting priority: archery, badminton, boxing, hockey, shooting and wrestling.Subsequently, Target Asian Games Group (TAGG), which was created last year to provide support to select athletes was disbanded this year. It had begun with an initial pool of 16 disciplines and 37 athletes.However, its responsibilities will now be shared between TOPS and Training of Elite Athletes and Management Support (TEAMS) divisions. TOPS and TEAMS will manage day-to-day operations, development, and coordination for 27 specific disciplines.TOPS selects athletes based on their medal potential rather than a single qualifying criterion. The scheme assesses recent international performances, world rankings, consistency at the elite level, long-term progression and potential to win medals at the Olympics and other major events. Recommendations from the Mission Olympic Cell (MOC), National Sports Federations (NSFs), coaches, foreign experts and sports science teams also play a key role.Athletes are divided into two categories:Core Group: Established athletes with immediate medal prospects.Development Group: Emerging athletes being prepared for future Olympic cycles.Their performances are monitored regularly to ensure support matches their progress.There is no fixed annual funding cap under TOPS. Instead, assistance is tailored to each athlete's requirements, depending on their sport, training programme and competition calendar.Funding can cover:For athletes in high-performance Olympic and Paralympic disciplines requiring overseas training and advanced support systems, annual funding can run into several lakhs or even crores of rupees. Every proposal undergoes technical and financial scrutiny before approval by the MOC.TOPS follows a two-pronged approach—backing athletes capable of winning medals immediately while simultaneously investing in future prospects.This is achieved through:The objective is to maximise India's medal chances today while creating a pipeline of athletes for future Olympic, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games and Paralympic cycles.Athletes are monitored continuously, with periodic reviews conducted by the Mission Olympic Cell alongside NSFs, coaches and technical experts.Reviews consider:TOPS follows a performance-linked funding model. If an athlete consistently underperforms, remains inactive without valid reasons or repeatedly misses agreed benchmarks, financial support can be reduced or withdrawn after evaluation.However, genuine circumstances such as injuries, rehabilitation or long-term planning are also taken into account before any decision is made.Yes. TOPS has expanded beyond traditional funding to provide a comprehensive high-performance support system.Support can include:The aim is to give Indian athletes access to the same integrated support systems available in leading sporting nations, with greater emphasis on recovery, injury management, mental resilience and scientific preparation.TOPS says its funding decisions are guided by transparency, accountability and merit. Every proposal passes through multiple stages of evaluation involving NSFs, coaches, sports science experts, the MOC and financial scrutiny under government procedures.Funding decisions are based on measurable criteria, including:The scheme also incorporates periodic reviews, stakeholder consultations, documented approval processes and audit mechanisms to ensure public funds are used effectively. Its stated vision is that no Indian athlete with genuine medal potential should miss out on world-class preparation because of financial constraints.It is now 10 years to the 2036 Olympics, a Summer Games that India intends to host in Ahmedabad. If awarded, the goal there will not just be showcase its culture and ability to host an event of such scale but to compete with the best. To that end, the Union Cabinet has approved a revamped Khelo India Scheme and enhanced assistance to National Sports Federations (NSFs).For the period of 2026-27 to 2030-31, which covers the 2030 CWG, LA 2028, Brisbane 2032 and five years leading to the 2036 Summer Games, a combined outlay of Rs 36,441 crore has been planned - Rs 29,054 crore towards Khelo India Scheme and Rs 7,387 crore to the NSFs.The revamped, and enhanced, Khelo India Scheme is nearly eight times the previous budget allocation (Rs 2532.22 crore from 2021-2026) towards grassroots development.After the positive returns at the Commonwealth Games, a tougher test awaits the Indian contingent later in the year at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan from September 19. And then further down the line at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, the necessary off-the-field steps for which have already been taken.

Article Title: 'A coterie hijacked him': Report claims Pakistan federation distanced itself from Arshad Nadeem before CWG flop
Article Text:
Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem (PTI Photo)

Federation 'distanced itself' from Olympic champion's preparations

Pakistan sporting structure under scrutiny

'A coterie hijacked him': Mentors question Nadeem's preparation

Pakistan's Olympic champion Arshad Nadeem has found himself at the centre of growing criticism following his disappointing Commonwealth Games campaign in Glasgow, with questions now being raised not just about his form but also about the support system that surrounded him in the lead-up to the competition.The defending Commonwealth Games champion endured one of the worst outings of his career, finishing ninth after failing to produce a throw beyond 80 metres. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage clinched the gold medal, while India's Neeraj Chopra and Yashvir Singh completed a historic South Asian podium with silver and bronze respectively.But as scrutiny intensified over Nadeem's performance, reports from Pakistan suggested the Olympic champion had effectively been left to prepare on his own after the Pakistan Amateur Athletics Federation (PAAF) allegedly distanced itself from his training programme following a dispute over the retention of his long-time coach Salman Butt According to a PTI report, the PAAF largely withdrew support from the star javelin thrower after disagreements emerged last year over his coaching setup. The report claimed that several requests made by Nadeem regarding his training programme were not entertained, while the Pakistan Sports Board also did not release funds to facilitate foreign coaches or trainers.Instead of training overseas under renowned South African coach Terseus Liebenberg, who had guided him before his Olympic triumph, Nadeem spent his Commonwealth Games build-up in Lahore with Salman Butt and local trainers.The contrast with India's preparation was striking. While Neeraj Chopra completed his final rehabilitation and training block in Biel, Switzerland, fellow Indian javelin throwers Yashvir Singh and Rohit Yadav trained in Spala, Poland, alongside foreign coaches and support staff before heading to Glasgow.The differing approaches were reflected in the final standings as India secured two medals, while Nadeem failed to qualify among the top eight after the opening three rounds.Nadeem had arrived in Glasgow with limited competitive exposure, having competed in only one preparatory meet in Switzerland during 2026. He also trained almost exclusively in Lahore despite the vastly different weather conditions between Pakistan and Scotland.His long-time coach Salman Butt admitted the Olympic champion was far from his best and acknowledged he was underprepared for the Games.Former Pakistan Athletics Federation president Akram Sahi also blamed negligence and inadequate preparation for the dramatic decline."Since Nadeem's Olympic gold medal a coterie has hijacked him and never let him come to me," Sahi told Telecom Asia Sport."This result in Glasgow is hugely disappointing... the signs were imminent for the last several months as there was negligence and lack of training."Another mentor, speaking anonymously, argued that Nadeem had become complacent and failed to invest sufficiently in elite overseas training after receiving substantial financial rewards following his Olympic success.Nadeem's disappointing campaign has reignited debate over Pakistan's sporting ecosystem.Former Olympic boxing bronze medallist Hussain Shah described the situation as a reflection of systemic shortcomings."This is an athlete who is self-made and comes from a village and belongs to a low-income family. But he brought so much glory to Pakistan with his gold medals. And yet he couldn't prepare properly for the CWG. It is a sad reflection on our sports structure," Shah said.Pakistan's campaign in Glasgow also exposed wider concerns. Boxer Fatima Zehra, who secured the country's only medal with bronze, also lamented the lack of quality preparation and international exposure, saying better training could have helped her challenge for gold.The criticism did not stop with Pakistan's athletics authorities. Two of Nadeem's former mentors also questioned the Olympic champion's preparation, alleging that a lack of quality training and poor decisions contributed to his disappointing campaign.Akram Sahi, the former Pakistan Athletics Federation president who helped identify Nadeem's talent in 2018, claimed the warning signs had been visible for months."Since Nadeem's Olympic gold medal a coterie has hijacked him and never let him come to me," Sahi told Telecom Asia Sport."This result in Glasgow is hugely disappointing for someone who has risen to new heights, but the signs were imminent for the last several months as there was negligence and lack of training."Another mentor, speaking anonymously, echoed those concerns, suggesting Nadeem had not trained adequately after returning from Haj and had become overly dependent on official support."He won the Olympics after he got extensive training from his South African coach Terseus Liebenberg. His training stints at Northwest University Potchefstroom also helped him clinch Olympic gold. Now he waited for the federation and government to send him to South Africa for training.He should have invested in himself rather than waiting for someone else," the mentor said.The mentor also questioned Nadeem's current coaching setup, claiming his long-time coach Salman Butt lacked specialist expertise in javelin and that the Olympic champion had become distracted by business ventures after receiving substantial financial rewards following his Paris triumph.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Olympic champion Arshad Nadeem finished ninth in the javelin throw at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Reports suggest the Pakistan Amateur Athletics Federation (PAAF) 'distanced itself' from his training programme following a dispute over the retention of his long-time coach Salman Butt. Former Pakistan Athletics Federation president Akram Sahi blamed negligence and inadequate preparation for the dramatic decline. Former Olympic boxing bronze medallist Hussain Shah described the situation as a reflection of systemic shortcomings.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Relay flop raises Asian Games alarm
Article Text:
Vishal TK (PTI Photo)

BENGALURU: Even as India celebrated a strong athletics campaign at the Commonwealth Games — highlighted by three para athletics gold medals to go with five silver and five bronze from the able-bodied contingent — attention has now shifted to the disappointing performance of the mixed 4x400m relay team.The quartet, which made the cut after surviving a rigorous selection process that saw the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) reject all the other relay combinations, failed to deliver on the biggest stage.Vishal TK, who set a national record this season with a personal best of 44.98 seconds in May, clocked a below-par 46.1 in the opening lap in the final. Ansa Babu then struggled to match the quality of the field, clocking 54.1 while rivals, led by Jamaica’s Leah Anderson (50.8 seconds), comfortably ran under 52 seconds.Santosh Kumar Tamilarasan (46.4 seconds) and Rashdeep Kaur (53.72 seconds) were unable to change the complexion of the race as India finished sixth and last in the final rankings after Australia was disqualified and Zambia failed to finish.“It seems India’s top runners peaked too early this season. Rajesh ran 45.26 in March but his performance dipped in Glasgow. Rajesh is one of our key relay runners and, with Mohammed Anas and Amoj Jacob still recovering from injuries, he is now the most experienced member of the squad.It will take a miracle for our relay runners to improve enough before the Asian Games next month,” another coach said.Rajesh, who clocked 47.00 seconds in the heats, was replaced by Santosh for the final. Several coaches who monitored the team’s preparations also questioned whether the expertise of foreign coach Jason Alexander Dawson was being fully utilised.“Two coaches training two separate groups of athletes simply doesn’t work. Whoever can’t cope with Jason’s workload shifts to the Indian coach. Ideally, all the 400m runners should train under one programme and one brain,” one coach said, referring to the parallel coaching setup under Dawson and Raj Mohan in Thiruvananthapuram.A former national coach, who had previously handled the relay squad, urged patience. “You can’t call Vishal a sub-45 runner unless he consistently runs below 45 seconds. I’m optimistic our relay squads will bounce back and perform well at the Asian Games. Earlier, India was stronger in the women’s 4x400m relay, but now the men’s team has become more competitive,” he said.Meanwhile, AFI has reportedly decided not to field the men’s 4x100m relay team at the Asian Games while clearing the remaining relay squads.

Article Title: Glasgow done, all eyes on 'Amdavad 2030': India's campaign offers both promise and warning signs
Article Text:
Indian boxer Jaismine Lamboria and other athletes during the closing ceremony of the CWG 2026. (PTI Photo)

Athletics leads the way



Boxers make a statement

PUNE: The Glasgow Commonwealth Games are over. The baton passes to India for the Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad, dubbed ‘Amdavad 2030’. With the event returning home after 20 years, India will be aiming not only to stage a better Games than Delhi 2010 but also to improve on its best-ever medal haul. At the 2010 Delhi Games, India won a record 101 medals to finish second in the overall standings.For Indian sport, Glasgow offered a mixed picture. The 39 medals collected this time were fewer than the 61 in Birmingham 2022, 66 in Gold Coast 2018 and 64 in Glasgow 2014. More importantly, those medals came from just six sports. By contrast, India’s medals had come from 17 sports in 2010, 11 in 2014, 15 in 2018 and 13 in 2022.The explanation lies partly in the programme itself. Glasgow did not include sports where India has traditionally been strong. India has won 135 medals in shooting between 1966 and 2018, excluding the 1970 Edinburgh edition. Wrestling has fetched India 114 medals across 18 editions since 1934. Yet Glasgow had no shooting, wrestling, hockey, badminton, archery or table tennis, which together had contributed 67 medals for India in Delhi 2010.As India prepares to host in 2030, the focus will be on retaining the positives from Glasgow while also bringing back its strongest disciplines.Athletics emerged as the biggest winner for India, with medals in the men’s 10,000m and 5,000m long jump, decathlon, high jump, triple jump and para-athletics adding up to 16 medals. What stood out most was the history made by Gulveer Singh, who won silver in the 10,000m and bronze in the 5,000m and Tejaswin Shankar, who claimed decathlon bronze.Yash Vir Singh also broke new ground by winning a javelin bronze in a field featuring Olympic and world champions, as well as world leaders and record holders. The para-athletes contributed three gold, two silver and one bronze, even as the 4x400m relay team had to settle for sixth place.“The performance was way better than expected. This has been a good result and it will only improve in the years to come. The result reflects the policies that the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) has adopted in the past few years,” former World Championships bronze medallist and current AFI senior vice-president Anju Bobby George told TOI.“Now we plan the training programme according to individual athletes’ requirements rather than designing a blanket programme for everyone. Some athletes train in the USA, some in Europe, because that is what best suits their future. The results are definitely going to improve in 2030 and beyond, as we also plan to host the Olympics,” she added.Boxing also delivered strongly, with seven gold among the 13 medals won. While the level of competition at the Commonwealth Games is not as demanding as at the Asian Games or Olympics, the performances will still provide a valuable confidence boost.“It is not as if these were the only medals our boxers have won so far. We had world champions, an Olympic medallist and Asian Games and Asian Championships winners at the Glasgow CWG. The field may not have been as strong as the Asiad, but it was not weak either.A good show at a competition like this gives a boost to the boxers,” 2008 Beijing Olympics bronze medallist Vijender Singh told TOI.With two historic gold and three medals overall, Indian judokas Asmita Dey, Harsh Singh and Yamini Mourya also deserve special mention. A sport that has often struggled for attention in the past appears to be finding its footing.If judo can continue on this trajectory, the possibilities are immense. With 15 medal events at the Olympics and proper investment and a cleaner administrative setup, India has genuine medal potential at the world level too.
Article Summary: Athletics emerged as the biggest winner for India, with medals in the men’s 10,000m and 5,000M long jump, decathlon, high jump, triple jump and para- athletics adding up to 16 medals. Boxing also delivered strongly, with seven gold among the 13 medals won. Judo also deserves special mention, with two historic gold and three medals overall.

Article Title: Spain's Bernabéu 'preferred' for 2030 World Cup final ahead of Morocco's much larger 115,000-seat stadium, says report
Article Text:
Bernabéu reportedly leads race for 2030 World Cup final, ahead of Morocco's ambitious 115,000-seat stadium plan.

Spanish broadcaster reports Bernabéu is FIFA's preferred choice

Spanish government expresses confidence

FIFA continues to reject earlier Morocco claims

The Times

Decision still awaits official confirmation

The race to host the 2030 FIFA World Cup final appears to have taken another significant turn, with fresh reports suggesting Real Madrid's Santiago Bernabéu has moved into pole position to stage football's biggest match. Although FIFA has yet to announce an official decision, recent developments from Spain have strengthened the belief that Madrid is currently leading the contest ahead of Morocco's proposed Hassan II Stadium.Spanish public broadcaster Radio Nacional de España (RNE) reported on Thursday that the Santiago Bernabéu is currently FIFA's preferred venue for the 2030 World Cup final.According to RNE, Morocco could instead be offered the opportunity to host the 2029 FIFA Club World Cup, a move the broadcaster presented as a way of recognising the North African nation's growing importance in international football while maintaining balance within the joint hosting arrangement.RNE's report comes after months of competition between Spain and Morocco over staging the tournament's showpiece fixture. Morocco has been promoting its under-construction 115,000-seat Hassan II Stadium near Casablanca, while Spain has put forward the renovated Santiago Bernabéu as its leading candidate.Neither FIFA nor the joint organising structure involving Spain, Portugal and Morocco has officially confirmed RNE's claims.FIFA has also not announced a bidding process or selected a host for the 2029 Club World Cup, with Brazil among the countries that have publicly expressed interest in staging that tournament.Separately, Spain's Sports Minister Milagros Tolón also expressed confidence that the final would ultimately be played in Spain.Speaking to Cadena SER, Tolón said:"We are the reigning men's and women's World Cup champions, and Spain and Portugal spearheaded the bid for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco later joined. We have many advantages and strengths as a country."The minister also referred to recent speculation surrounding the final venue, saying the Spanish government had been surprised by earlier reports but welcomed FIFA's subsequent clarification."The most important thing is that FIFA has already denied it. We are working with FIFA, and we have our next meeting in September. They have been very clear and emphatic in denying this news. We will continue working because we want the World Cup final to be in Spain."The latest reports follow claims published earlier this week by, which alleged FIFA president Gianni Infantino had privately offered Morocco the right to host the 2030 World Cup final in exchange for political backing as pressure mounted over his leadership.FIFA strongly rejected those allegations, with a spokesperson describing the report as "false and misleading" and insisting no promise had been made regarding the final venue. The governing body added that a decision on where the final will be staged would be made "in due course."Spain, Portugal and Morocco will jointly stage the centenary edition of the FIFA World Cup in 2030, while Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay will each host one commemorative opening match to mark 100 years since the inaugural tournament.Although RNE now reports that the renovated Bernabéu, a 85,000-seat stadium, has emerged as FIFA's preferred venue and the Spanish government remains optimistic about hosting the final, the selection has not yet been officially confirmed.For now, Madrid appears to have gained momentum in the race, but until FIFA formally announces the venue, both the Santiago Bernabéu and Morocco's Hassan II Stadium remain part of the conversation surrounding where the 2030 World Cup will ultimately crown its next champions.
Article Summary: Real Madrid's Santiago Bernabéu reportedly leads race for 2030 World Cup final, ahead of Morocco's ambitious 115,000-seat stadium plan. Spain's Sports Minister Milagros Tolón also expressed confidence that the final would ultimately be played in Spain. FIFA continues to reject earlier Morocco claims.
